items.headline: National Academies rank four non‑polar lunar sites for crewed missions
items.title: National Academies Rank Nonpolar Moon Sites
items.scifi_hook: Astronauts could step onto the far‑side Bhabha Crater, shielded from Earth’s radio chatter.
items.eli5: A science panel listed the best non‑pole spots on the Moon for short astronaut trips.
items.why: It directs future NASA missions to locations with high scientific payoff.
items.text: Location, location, location is everything—even on the Moon. Astronauts are heading back to the lunar surface, and now the scientific community has made its voice heard on where they should go with the release yesterday of a National Academies report ranking the top four non-polar sites for future crewed lunar missions. NASA asked the committee which science goals in locations beyond the poles need people rather than robots, and where to send those astronauts. The committee’s answer assumes short sorties: two-person crews, no rover, and one to four moonwalks per site. Sites were weighed on three criteria: whether science aligned with the decadal surveys and NASA’s Moon to Mars objectives, if the missions would expand US exploration capabilities, and, to a lesser degree, how they would contribute to public inspiration. Site seeing: The sites, in priority order: Bhabha Crater: Astronauts have never landed this far from Earth. The far-side crater sits in the middle of the South Pole-Aitken Basin, which may have the oldest impact signature in the solar system. The region is also shielded from Earth’s radio noise, making it a prime spot for low-frequency astronomy. Mons Hadley: Apollo 11 and 17 are seen by NASA as protected heritage sites because of their historical significance, so the committee picked the Apollo 15 site instead. items.headline: Hudbay and Mitsubishi approve development of Arizona’s Copper World project
items.title: Hudbay, Mitsubishi greenlight Copper World project development in Arizona
items.scifi_hook: A massive open‑pit copper mine could start producing in 2029, boosting U.S. metal supply.
items.eli5: Hudbay and Mitsubishi will build a large copper mine in Arizona, aiming for 102,000 tonnes per year.
items.why: It adds a domestic source of copper critical for electrification and renewable tech.
items.text: Hudbay Minerals Inc and its partner Mitsubishi Corporation have approved the development of what they say will be one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the US. The news came when announcing the results of the definitive feasibility study and related prefeasibility studies (collectively referred to as ‘the DFS’) for the Copper World project, 70% owned by Hudbay and 30% owned by Mitsubishi. With first production projected in the second half of 2029, Copper World will be the first of the next generation of long-life, low-cost copper mines in the Americas, Hudbay claims. The DFS outlines annual copper production of 102,000 t over the first 10 years, an 11% increase when compared to 92,000 t in Hudbay’s 2023 prefeasibility study for Copper World. This could see Hudbay’s consolidated annual copper production increase to approximately 250,000 t, doubling current production levels, with other brownfield growth projects underway. The base case for Copper World contemplates a 15-year mine life utilising mineral reserves (390 Mt at 0.47% Cu), and requires only state and local permits, This base case further optimises the 2023 PFS mine plan with an in-pit crushing and conveying (IPCC) system in year four and an expansion of the concentrator from 54,431 t/d to 81,64t t/d in year five.
